name: Yocto Project

foundation.via: A Linux Foundation project that shares BitBake and OpenEmbedded-Core with the OpenEmbedded community

license: Metadata MIT; BitBake GPL-2.0-only; each recipe’s software under its own licence
summary: Tools and metadata for building your own Linux distribution for an embedded device, from source: kernel, toolchain, packages, root filesystem image and SDK, reproducibly and with licence records.
intro: The Yocto Project is not a Linux distribution but a way to make one. Its build system, the OpenEmbedded build system, is driven by BitBake, a task scheduler that reads metadata and runs fetch, patch, configure, compile, package and image tasks in parallel. The metadata is mostly recipes (`.bb` files), each saying where a piece of software’s source comes from, which patches to apply, what it depends on and how to build it, and configuration that picks a target `MACHINE` and a `DISTRO` policy. Recipes are grouped into layers stacked in a set order: OpenEmbedded-Core for the essentials, a board support package (BSP) layer from the chip or board vendor, distribution and application layers of your own, with `.bbappend` files adjusting other layers’ recipes without editing them. From one build you get a cross toolchain, a kernel, packages in RPM, DEB or IPK format, a root filesystem image for the board and an SDK for application developers. Poky, defined in the `meta-yocto` layer, is the reference distribution used for testing and as a starting point; the project says it is not meant to be shipped as a product as it is.

Two features make it practical at scale. The shared state (sstate) cache stores each task’s output under a signature of its inputs, so later builds, on the same machine or from a shared mirror, reuse everything that hasn’t changed; and builds are reproducible, 99.8% for the `core-image-minimal` image. Every build also records the licence of each package and can emit SPDX SBOMs, which product teams use for compliance and, since 6.0, post-build CVE checks with `sbom-cve-check`. A new version comes out every six months, and every two years one is a long-term support (LTS) release with four years of support: 5.0 Scarthgap (April 2024, supported to April 2028) and 6.0 Wrynose (April 2026, supported to April 2030, with Linux 6.18 and GCC 15.2). 6.1 Blacksail was tagged on October 20, 2026. The combined `poky` repository is no longer updated for new releases: since 5.3 you set up a build with `bitbake-setup`, which fetches the layers you choose, or clone BitBake, OpenEmbedded-Core and `meta-yocto` separately. Wind River Linux, MontaVista and Siemens’ (formerly Mentor’s) embedded Linux products are built with it.
strengths: Full control of the image: you choose every package, version, compile option and init system, and get a minimal root filesystem for exactly one board
Silicon vendors ship BSP layers for it, so new boards usually come with a ready Yocto layer
Reproducible, cached builds: sstate reuses unchanged task outputs across machines, and identical inputs give near-identical binaries
Compliance built in: licence manifests, source archives and SPDX SBOMs come out of every build, and LTS releases get four years of fixes
limits: Steep learning curve: BitBake’s syntax, variable overrides, layer priorities and task dependencies take time to learn, and errors can be hard to trace
Heavy first builds: the 6.x quick start asks for at least 140 GB of disk, 32 GB of RAM and 16 cores, and a build from scratch compiles the whole toolchain and distribution
You own the distribution: security updates, kernel patches and package upgrades are yours to track and rebuild, unlike a general-purpose distribution
Releases outside the LTS line get only six months of support, so products should follow an LTS branch and plan migrations every two to four years

story: In 2001 Sharp’s Zaurus PDA shipped with embedded Linux, and Chris Larson founded OpenZaurus to replace its software, using the Buildroot build system. In January 2003 Larson, Michael Lauer and Holger Schurig started a more general build system for embedded Linux, OpenEmbedded, by porting hundreds of OpenZaurus packages to it; its task runner, BitBake, was inspired by Gentoo’s Portage. Richard Purdie built Poky as a stabilised branch of OpenEmbedded, with a core set of recipes for a limited set of architectures, at OpenedHand, which Intel bought in 2008.

Embedded Linux developers still faced different build systems and software from one architecture and vendor to the next. In October 2010 the Linux Foundation announced the Yocto Project to give them more consistent software and tools across architectures, built on Poky. It agreed to work with OpenEmbedded on a shared core, OpenEmbedded-Core, maintained together with BitBake. Release 1.0 followed on April 6, 2011, with a steering group of Dell, Intel, Mentor Graphics, OpenEmbedded e.V., Texas Instruments, Timesys and Wind River.

The project settled into two releases a year with LTS versions every two years, and added sstate mirrors, SPDX SBOMs and CVE tooling as compliance became part of shipping a device. In 2025 it stopped updating the combined `poky` repository for new releases in favour of `bitbake-setup`.

choices.choice: A build system, not a distribution
choices.why: Embedded products differ in hardware, size and licensing needs, so the project ships the means to build a tailored distribution, with Poky only as a reference, instead of one image for everyone.

Separating BSP, distribution and application metadata lets a vendor’s board support, a company’s policy and a product’s software be maintained by different people and combined, with `.bbappend` files changing other layers without forking them.
Rather than compete with OpenEmbedded, the Yocto Project agreed on a common, tested core metadata set, OE-Core, so both communities maintain one set of essential recipes and one BitBake.
Compiling a whole distribution takes hours. Storing each task’s output under a signature of its inputs lets builds reuse results from earlier builds or a shared mirror and rebuild only what changed.
